title: BELA Act 1: What changed and why
description: What the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act 32 of 2024 is, why it was passed, when it came into force and a quick map of its main changes.

lessons.title: What the BELA Act is
lessons.summary: The Basic Education Laws Amendment Act 32 of 2024 in plain English: what it amends and who it affects.
lessons.body:
## 📜 A short name for a big change

The Basic Education Laws Amendment Act 32 of 2024 is usually called the **BELA Act**. It is not a brand new school law. It is an amending Act: it changes the wording of two existing laws that SGBs, boards of governors and principals already work with every day.

1. The **South African Schools Act 84 of 1996 (SASA)**. This is the main law on learners, admission, language, governing bodies and school money.
2. The **Employment of Educators Act 76 of 1998**. This deals with the employment of educators. BELA sections 41 to 53 amend it.

So when you read "BELA s4", that means section 4 of the amending Act. When you read "SASA s5", that means section 5 of the Schools Act as it reads now, after BELA changed it. In this course we cite both, for example "SASA s3(1) as amended by BELA s2".

## 🧩 How an amending Act is built

The BELA Act has 54 sections. Most of them say something like "Section 8 of the South African Schools Act is hereby amended by...". In the official Gazette version, words in bold square brackets are words that were deleted, and underlined words are new words. That is why the BELA Act on its own can be hard to read.

> 💡 Tip: Do not try to read the BELA Act on its own. Read the consolidated (updated) version of SASA that shows the law as it stands today. The Department of Basic Education publishes a version of SASA "as amended by BELA 2024" on its website.

## 🏫 Who does it affect?

Most BELA changes are aimed at **public schools**, because SASA gives public school governing bodies their powers. Examples are the code of conduct for learners (SASA s8), admission policy (SASA s5) and language policy (SASA s6).

Some changes reach **all schools**, public and independent. SASA defines a "school" as a public school or an independent school (SASA s1). So rules that apply "at a school" also apply at independent schools. The ban on corporal punishment (SASA s10) and on initiation practices (SASA s10A) are good examples. The compulsory attendance rule in SASA s3 is about every learner, whatever school they attend.

There are also a few changes aimed only at **independent schools**. The long title of the BELA Act says it increases the penalty for running an independent school that is not registered, and lets the MEC set conditions when a subsidy is given to an independent school.

> ⚠️ Watch out: If you sit on a board of governors at an independent school, do not assume BELA does not apply to you. Check each change: does it say "public school", or does it say "school"?

## 🗂️ What the Act itself says it does

Every Act starts with a "long title" that lists what it does. The BELA long title is long, but in summary it covers:

- compulsory Grade R and stronger penalties for keeping a learner out of school
- admission and language policy, with more say for the Head of Department (HOD)
- the code of conduct, learner discipline, drugs and liquor, suspension and expulsion
- corporal punishment and initiation practices
- SGB governance, conflicts of interest, finances and reporting
- home education (home schooling)
- new offences, a dispute resolution process and new powers for the Minister to make regulations

Lesson 4 gives you the main changes at a glance.

## ✅ Key points

- The BELA Act (Act 32 of 2024) amends SASA (Act 84 of 1996) and the Employment of Educators Act (Act 76 of 1998).
- "BELA s4" means the amending section; "SASA s5" means the Schools Act as it now reads.
- Read the consolidated SASA, not the BELA Act on its own.
- Many changes apply to public schools only, but rules that apply "at a school" also bind independent schools.

lessons.title: Why it was passed
lessons.summary: The problems the BELA Act was meant to fix, and why it was so hotly debated.
lessons.body:
## 🎯 Why change a law from 1996?

SASA was passed in 1996, two years after democracy. It has been amended several times since then, but by the 2010s government said parts of it no longer matched what was happening in schools. The Department of Basic Education brought the Basic Education Laws Amendment Bill to Parliament as Bill B2 of 2022. After public hearings in Parliament and the NCOP, it became the BELA Act in 2024.

You do not need to know every step of that history. What matters for an SGB or board of governors is the set of problems the Act targets. The best evidence of the purpose is the Act's own long title.

## 🧒 1. Getting children into school earlier and keeping them there

Grade R was widely offered but was not compulsory. The Act now makes school attendance compulsory from Grade R (SASA s3(1) as amended by BELA s2). It also raises the penalty for a parent, or anyone else, who keeps a learner out of school without just cause (SASA s3(6)) and makes it an offence to disrupt a school's official educational activities (SASA s3(7)).

## 🚪 2. Fair access to schools

Government argued that some admission and language policies kept learners out of schools with space. BELA gives the HOD the final say on admission after consulting the governing body (SASA s5, BELA s4), and lets the HOD direct a school to offer more than one language of instruction where practicable (SASA s6, BELA s5). These two sections caused the most public debate. They are covered in BELA 3.

## 🛡️ 3. Protecting learners

The Act tightens rules on learner discipline. It requires a code of conduct to respect diverse cultural beliefs, religious observances and medical circumstances (SASA s8(2), BELA s7), refines suspension and expulsion (SASA s9, BELA s9), and clearly abolishes corporal punishment, including in school hostels (SASA s10, BELA s10). BELA 2 covers this.

## 💰 4. Accountability for governance and money

The long title lists many governance changes: declaring personal and financial interests and recusal, who may chair the finance committee, HOD approval of some leases, financial statements, and quarterly income and expenditure reports to the HOD. BELA 4 covers these.

## 🏠 5. Regulating home education

Home schooling grew, but the rules were thin. The Act replaces SASA s51 with a fuller registration process for home education (BELA s35).

> 💡 Tip: When a parent at your school says "BELA takes away the SGB's powers", it helps to know the balance. The SGB still adopts the admission policy, the language policy and the code of conduct. What changed is that the HOD now has stronger oversight and the final say in certain cases.

## 🗣️ Why it was controversial

Supporters said the Act promotes access, equality and learner safety. Critics, including some governing body associations, unions, parties in the Government of National Unity and civil society groups, raised concerns. The biggest fights were about admission and language (Afrikaans schools in particular), home education and the balance of power between the HOD and SGBs. That debate is why the President delayed part of the Act when he signed it, as Lesson 3 explains.

> ⚠️ Watch out: Public debate is not law. When a parent quotes a news story or social media post, check what SASA actually says now.

## ✅ Key points

- The BELA Bill was Bill B2 of 2022 and became Act 32 of 2024.
- Its aims include compulsory Grade R, fairer access, learner protection, better governance and regulated home education.
- Admission (SASA s5) and language (SASA s6) were the most debated changes.
- SGBs and boards keep most of their policy roles, but the HOD gained more oversight.

lessons.title: When it was signed and when it started
lessons.summary: Signed in September 2024, in force from 24 December 2024, with the story of the delayed admission and language sections.
lessons.body:
## 📅 Signing is not the same as starting

An Act can be signed on one day and come into force on another. The BELA Act says so itself: it comes into operation on a date fixed by the President by proclamation in the Government Gazette (BELA s54).

## 🖊️ Step 1: Assent in September 2024

- The President assented to (signed) the BELA Act on **13 September 2024**.
- It was published in Government Gazette No. 51258 on **16 September 2024**.

When he signed, the President announced that the implementation of **sections 4 and 5** of the Act would be delayed by three months, so that parties in the Government of National Unity could try to agree on them. BELA s4 amends SASA s5 (admission). BELA s5 amends SASA s6 (language policy).

Some legal organisations pointed out at the time that, strictly speaking, none of the Act was yet in force, because no commencement proclamation had been published. That is a useful reminder: under BELA s54, nothing starts until the proclamation.

## 📣 Step 2: The proclamation in December 2024

- On **20 December 2024** the President announced that he had signed a proclamation to bring the Act into operation, **including sections 4 and 5**, without amendments.
- The proclamation was published as Proclamation Notice 237 of 2024 in Government Gazette No. 51836 of **24 December 2024**.
- The Department of Basic Education has confirmed in a reply to a parliamentary question (NW1483 of 2025) that the Act commenced on 24 December 2024.

So the answer to "Are the admission and language sections in force?" is **yes**. The whole Act has been law since 24 December 2024. You may see 20 December 2024 in some news reports. That is the date of the announcement and signature of the proclamation. The commencement date in the Gazette is 24 December 2024.

> 💡 Tip: If an SGB member says "the language clause was suspended", explain that the delay applied only from September to December 2024. Since 24 December 2024 all 54 sections are in force.

## 📘 Step 3: Regulations and guidelines

The President asked the Minister of Basic Education to prepare regulations and norms and standards to support the Act. In its parliamentary reply the department said that none of the Act's sections depend on regulations before they apply. In other words, the law applies now, even where detailed regulations are still being finalised.

What has happened since:

- In June 2025 the Minister issued interim implementation guidelines, mainly on admission and language policies.
- On 6 August 2025 the first two sets of draft regulations were published for public comment: draft regulations on the admission of learners to public schools (Gazette No. 53119) and draft minimum uniform norms and standards on capacity (Gazette No. 53120).
- Other regulations, for example on home education, were still being prepared.

> ⚠️ Watch out: Regulations move faster than training material. Before your SGB or board relies on a regulation or guideline, ask your district office, or your provincial department for independent schools, which version is current and whether it is final or still a draft. Some organisations also announced court challenges to the Act in 2025, so check whether any court order affects your school.

## ✅ Key points

- Assent: 13 September 2024. Published: Gazette No. 51258, 16 September 2024.
- Sections 4 (admission) and 5 (language) were held back for three months while parties consulted.
- The whole Act, including sections 4 and 5, commenced on 24 December 2024 (Proclamation 237 of 2024, Gazette No. 51836).
- The Act applies now; regulations and guidelines add detail. Always check the current version with your district.

lessons.title: The big changes at a glance
lessons.summary: A quick map of what BELA changed, so you know where to look and which module covers it.
lessons.body:
## 🗺️ Your map of BELA

This lesson is a checklist. Use it at an SGB or board meeting when someone asks "Does BELA say anything about...?". The other BELA modules go deeper.

## 🎒 Learners and attendance (BELA 2)

- **Compulsory Grade R.** Every parent must cause their child to attend school from Grade R, starting in the year the child turns six, until the year the child turns 15 or completes Grade 9, whichever comes first (SASA s3(1) as amended by BELA s2). Before BELA, compulsory school started at age seven.
- **Higher penalties.** A parent who, after a written notice from the HOD, keeps a learner out of school without just cause, or anyone else who prevents a learner from attending, can be fined or jailed for up to 12 months. It used to be six months (SASA s3(6)).
- **New offence of disrupting school.** Anyone who unlawfully and intentionally interrupts, disturbs or hinders a school's official educational activities commits an offence, with up to 12 months (SASA s3(7)).
- **Monitoring attendance.** Educators, the principal and the governing body must promote and monitor attendance. After three consecutive days of unexplained absence the class teacher reports to the principal (SASA s4A, inserted by BELA s3).

## ⚖️ Discipline and safety (BELA 2)

- **Code of conduct.** It must take into account learners' diverse cultural beliefs, religious observances and medical circumstances, include an exemption clause, and disciplinary proceedings must be age-appropriate and in the best interests of the learner (SASA s8 as amended by BELA s7).
- **Drugs and liquor.** The rules now refer to "a drug" or "any drug", not only "illegal" drugs, and a learner may face disciplinary proceedings if liquor or any drug is found on them or a test is positive (SASA s8A(12) as amended by BELA s8).
- **Suspension.** SASA s9(1) now lists serious misconduct, and requires immediate suspension where a learner is formally charged by SAPS with certain crimes at school (BELA s9).
- **Corporal punishment** is abolished, including during school activities and in hostels (SASA s10, BELA s10). **Initiation practices** are banned during school activities too (SASA s10A, BELA s11).

## 🚪 Admission and language (BELA 3)

- The HOD has stronger authority over admission, after consulting the governing body (SASA s5, BELA s4).
- South African Sign Language has the status of an official language for learning at a public school, and the HOD may direct a public school to adopt more than one language of instruction where practicable (SASA s6, BELA s5).

## 🏛️ Governance and money (BELA 4)

The long title of the BELA Act lists, among other things: declaring interests and recusal by SGB members, clearer rules against paying SGB members, a parent member who is not employed at the school chairing the finance committee where reasonably practicable, HOD approval for leases of school property (except for leases not exceeding 12 months), financial statements presented to a parents' meeting, quarterly income and expenditure reports to the HOD, the HOD's power to dissolve a governing body that has stopped functioning, and a dispute resolution process between the HOD and a governing body (SASA s59A, inserted by BELA s37).

## 🧾 Other changes worth knowing

- **Home education** must be registered with the HOD (SASA s51 as substituted by BELA s35).
- **False information.** It is an offence to give false or misleading information, or a forged document, when applying for admission or for a fee exemption, with up to 12 months (SASA s59(3), added by BELA s36).
- **New regulation topics.** The Minister may now make regulations on, among others, the management of learner pregnancy and the admission of learners to public schools (SASA s61, as amended by BELA s39).

> 💡 Tip: Print this lesson's headings as a one-page "BELA map" for new SGB or board members at their induction.

> ⚠️ Watch out: This is a summary. Before you change a school policy, read the exact section in the consolidated SASA and check any current provincial circular with your district office.

## ✅ Key points

- Grade R is compulsory and the penalties for keeping a child out of school rose to 12 months.
- Discipline rules changed: code of conduct exemptions, drugs and liquor, suspension, corporal punishment and initiation.
- Admission and language: the HOD has more say (BELA 3).
- Governance and finances: more disclosure and reporting (BELA 4).

questions.text: Which two laws does the BELA Act amend?

options.text: The National Education Policy Act and the Children's Act
The South African Schools Act 84 of 1996 and the Employment of Educators Act 76 of 1998
The Public Finance Management Act and the South African Schools Act
The Employment of Educators Act and the Constitution

questions.explanation: The long title and sections of the BELA Act amend SASA (BELA ss1 to 40) and the Employment of Educators Act 76 of 1998 (BELA ss41 to 53).

questions.text: In this course, what does "SASA s5 as amended by BELA s4" mean?

options.text: Section 5 of the Schools Act as it now reads, changed by section 4 of the BELA Act
Section 4 of the Schools Act, which replaced section 5
A regulation numbered 5 made under section 4
Section 5 of the BELA Act, which amends section 4 of SASA

questions.explanation: BELA is an amending Act. BELA s4 is the amending section; SASA s5 is the Schools Act section on admission as it now reads.

questions.text: Why does the ban on corporal punishment also bind independent schools?

options.text: Because independent schools signed up to BELA voluntarily
Because the Minister issued a separate circular for independent schools
Because it does not bind them; it is for public schools only
Because SASA defines a "school" as a public or an independent school, and s10 applies at a school

questions.explanation: SASA s1 defines "school" to include independent schools. SASA s10 (as amended by BELA s10) bans corporal punishment at a school, during a school activity or in a hostel.

questions.text: On what date did the President assent to the BELA Act?

options.text: 24 December 2024
13 September 2024
1 January 2025
16 September 2024

questions.explanation: The Act records that it was assented to on 13 September 2024. It was published in Gazette No. 51258 on 16 September 2024.

questions.text: From what date has the whole BELA Act, including the admission and language sections, been in force?

options.text: 13 September 2024
1 January 2026, when regulations take effect
24 December 2024
It is not yet in force

questions.explanation: Under BELA s54 the Act commences on a date fixed by proclamation. Proclamation Notice 237 of 2024 (Gazette No. 51836) brought the whole Act into operation on 24 December 2024.

questions.text: Which SASA sections were affected by the three-month delay announced when the Act was signed?

options.text: SASA s5 (admission) and s6 (language policy), amended by BELA s4 and s5
SASA s3 (attendance) and s10 (corporal punishment)
SASA s51 (home education) and s59 (information)
SASA s8 (code of conduct) and s9 (suspension)

questions.explanation: The President delayed BELA sections 4 and 5 for consultation. BELA s4 amends SASA s5 (admission) and BELA s5 amends SASA s6 (language).

questions.text: A board member says the BELA Act cannot apply until all regulations are final. What did the Department of Basic Education say?

options.text: The Act applies only to schools that have adopted the regulations
The Act is suspended until the Constitutional Court rules
Only the governance sections apply before regulations
None of the Act's sections depend on regulations before they apply

questions.explanation: In parliamentary reply NW1483 of 2025 the department confirmed commencement on 24 December 2024 (under BELA s54) and that implementation is not contingent on regulations.

questions.text: What is the compulsory school-going period under SASA s3(1) as amended by BELA s2?

options.text: From Grade 1 in the year the child turns seven, until age 15
From Grade R in the year the child turns five, until Grade 12
From Grade R in the year the child turns six, until the year the child turns 15 or completes Grade 9, whichever comes first
From Grade R at age six until age 18

questions.explanation: SASA s3(1), as amended by BELA s2, starts compulsory attendance at Grade R in the year the learner turns six, ending in the year the learner turns 15 or completes Grade 9, whichever occurs first.

questions.text: Which new offence did BELA add to SASA s3?

options.text: Failing to pay school fees on time
Unlawfully and intentionally interrupting, disturbing or hindering a school's official educational activities
Refusing to serve on a governing body
Teaching in a language not in the language policy

questions.explanation: SASA s3(7), added by BELA s2(c), makes disruption of official educational activities an offence, with a fine or up to 12 months imprisonment.

questions.text: A parent gives a forged document to get a fee exemption. Under BELA, what is the position?

options.text: It is an offence, with a fine or up to 12 months imprisonment, under SASA s59(3)
It is only a matter for the code of conduct
The SGB may fine the parent directly
It is not an offence; the school may only refuse the exemption

questions.explanation: SASA s59(3), added by BELA s36, makes it an offence to submit false or misleading information or a forged document when applying for admission or fee exemption.
